lines.note: Completes Abano on f420: a fan gilded on both sides. The preceding page’s doura- is a catchword, not extra running text here.
Riôri directs the reader to the alternative spelling Reôri. Both Japanese forms are upright; Vide is italic Portuguese apparatus.
Riorit is musical consonance or harmony. The source spells armonia without an initial h and ends the Japanese word with bare t.
Ryōsoku denotes both feet, futatsu no ashi. The final S. is upright and separate from the Portuguese gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ryōten describes cool air or sky. The damaged synonym is read provisionally as Suſuxij ſora; the tall middle letter looks like long s, despite the expected lexical reading suzushii.
Ryōsha is a house or lodging, here specified as a Buddhist monk’s dwelling. The mark in Bǒzuno points downward and is retained as a caron.
The Portuguese specifies a monk’s cell or room. Bonzo is part of the Portuguese gloss, not an additional Japanese headword.

runs.text: Nouas que ſe contão de duas maneiras.

lines.note: Ryōsetsu is news told in two different versions. The checked final t belongs to the historical headword spelling.
The additional sense is two opinions. The unusual tilde placement in opinioẽs is retained rather than modernized.
Futari no tsukai refers to two messengers; the Portuguese gloss gives “two messages.” Preserve the source’s wording rather than harmonizing the two expressions.
Ryōshin here is a good retainer, yoi shinka. The Portuguese Bom criado supports the personal-service sense.
The next Ryōshin is a good or auspicious time, yoi toki. The Portuguese explanation continues with favorable augury below.
Completes the auspicious-time definition: a favorable occasion for doing something. The printed algũa remains unexpanded.
Ryōsho is two places, futatokoro, with a further application to two people. The scan restores Futatocoro and lugares, replacing OCR Futatocoto and ſugares; the headword has a caron.
Peßoas completes the second gloss, two people. The β-like double-s sort is retained as ß in line with the supplied diplomatic convention.
Ryōshō is two commanders, futari no taishō. Both marked vowels in the headword take carons, and Futarino corrects OCR Furarino.
The paragraph sign introduces ryōshō ei wo arasō, two commanders competing in power or splendor. The row ends with printed cõ.; no unverified hyphen is supplied.
Tendem continues the Portuguese verb across the line boundary, followed by rivalry over power and pomp. The provisional st spelling in fausto is retained.
The following Ryōshō instead means a good commander, yo(k)i taishō. Its separate entry and identical-looking pronunciation are preserved.
Ryōshu means both hands, futatsu no te. The damaged first u of Futatçuno is restored from the scan rather than read as a.
The second Ryōshu is a good lord or master. The Portuguese reads ſenhor, not OCR ſenhar; the final S. is upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ryōya is a fine night, yo(k)i yoru. The illustrative phrase begins Riǒ- and continues onto the next row.
Yauo moteaſobu completes enjoying a fine night. The Portuguese Gozarſe introduces the ways of enjoying it listed below.

runs.text: vendo a lũa, ou neue, praticando, &c. S.

lines.note: The examples are viewing the moon or snow and conversing. The final S. is the written-register label, outside the italic gloss.
Ryōyoku denotes two wings, futatsu no tsubasa. The headword is continuous Riǒyocu; the OCR’s internal space is not supported by the letter spacing.
Completes the gloss as both wings. The upright S. is a usage marker, not italic Portuguese. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ryōyū refers to two strong or valiant men. The example begins Riǒ- across the physical line division.
Yǔ completes the preceding headword in the maxim that two mighty men inevitably contend. The caron and u are visible where OCR gave yn.

runs.text: tes pella mòrparte contendem, ou competẽ. S.

lines.note: The Portuguese qualifies the maxim as such men generally contending or competing. The close spelling mòrparte and abbreviated competẽ are retained; S. is upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ryōzai means good timber, yo(k)i zaimoku. A damaged but present i restores Riǒzai from OCR Rǒzai.
Ryōzu denotes two heads. The headword’s doubled zz and following u are retained as printed in Riǒzzu.
Riken is a sharp sword, explained by surudona ken and tsurugi. Eſ- begins the divided Portuguese word for sword.
Pada completes Eſ-pada, specified as cutting well. The short continuation belongs to the preceding weapon entry.
Riki, alternatively rikisha, is a shaved attendant serving as a lance page. The scan restores the alternative marker l and the full Riqixa rather than OCR’s broken punctuation and iqixa.

runs.text: de pagem da lança, leuando hũa Naguinata

lines.note: The attendant carries a Naguinata, a Japanese weapon name embedded in Portuguese. Its italic setting is retained from the aligned draft after comparison with the surrounding gloss; the whole word is flagged for typeface review.
Diante do ſenhor specifies that the attendant precedes the lord. It completes the lance-page explanation.
Riki is strength, chikara. The paragraph sign introduces a phrase describing someone who possesses strength.
Monogia completes riki no aru mono ja, a strong person. The Portuguese explicitly says he is a man who has strength.
Rikiji is a strong man, chikara no otoko. The Portuguese for- is physically divided before çoſo.
Çoſo completes forçoſo, strong. The upright S. is a written-register label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Rikiryō means great strength, tsuyoi chikara. The Portuguese directly confirms the strength sense.
Rikiryōna mono describes a person of great strength. The scan restores the middle ri sequence in Riqiriǒna, which OCR reduced to Riqinǒna.
Forças completes Homem de grandes forças. This short physical row ends the preceding example.

Rikisha is a strong man; the Portuguese reads forçoſo. At the far right of this same physical row, the source prints the displaced cross-reference “( Riqi,” belonging with Vide ſupra below; it is retained in place without inventing a closing parenthesis.

runs.text: Hũ homẽ pagẽ da lança. Vide ſupra,

lines.note: The next Rikisha is a lance page, with Vide ſupra referring back to Riqi. The referenced word is physically displaced to the far right of the preceding row, not inserted into this row.
Riqua is a pear blossom, nashi no hana. The initial is R, not OCR B, and S. is upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Riquan is explained by Cutçu; camuri: footwear and a crown or head covering, as confirmed by the Portuguese continuing in the next column. Enlargement favors a damaged m in camuri rather than the draft n; this chosen reading is retained with caution, without expanding it to canmuri. The printed co- continues as roa there, completing coroa. The two Japanese explanations are separated by a printed semicolon.

runs.text: roa, ou outra couſa com que ſe cobre, & orna

lines.note: Roa completes co-roa from the preceding column: a crown or another article covering and adorning the head. The verb is cobre, not OCR cabre.
A cabeça completes the head-covering definition. The upright S. marks written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ririshii is lively and alert. The Portuguese reads viuo, retaining historical u/v, rather than OCR oiuo.
Ririxisa and ririxū are the noun/adverbial forms associated with the preceding adjective. Their upright type distinguishes them from the Portuguese apparatus.
Riron is discussion or argument, kotowari wo ronzuru. The Portuguese Diſputa directly supports the reasoning/debating sense.
Risai is keenness of intellect, surudona chiye. The Portuguese starts an explanation in terms of mental liveliness.
Agudeza adds sharpness; risaina hito begins the example of a sharp-minded person. The paragraph mark separates definition and example.
Completes the example as an acute and perceptive person. The long s in ſagaz is retained.
Risan means dispersing after separating, hanare chiru. The Portuguese eſpalhar- continues its reflexive ending on the next row.

runs.text: ſe, ou partirſe pera diuerſas partes. Vt,

lines.note: Completes dispersing or departing to various places. Vt introduces the Japanese verbal example on the following line.
Riſanſuru is the example “to disperse.” The joined spelling and the following upright S. are preserved. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Risō is pursuing one’s profit diligently. The scan shows a circumflex in Riſô and the printed phrase Rini vaxiru; the unusual initial v in vaxiru is not silently replaced.
Completes the profit-seeking definition: acting diligently for one’s own advantage and gain. Proueito and ganho are coordinated objects of the preceding activity.
Risu is described as a small animal resembling a ferret. The Portuguese comparison uses printed forão, not a modernized furão; it does not establish a precise species.
Rita means benefiting or saving others, ta wo sukuu. The gloss divides ou-tros across the physical boundary.
Tros completes outros, the people being saved or delivered. Bup. marks this as Buddhist terminology.
Ritan is identified with shōgatsu, the first moon or month. The synonym retains the bare checked final t in Xǒguat.
Do anno completes “the first month of the year.” It belongs to the preceding calendar entry.
Ritgui concerns uprightness or integrity, tadaxii koto. The Portuguese emphasizes simplicity and wholeness of character.
Inteireza completes the definition; ritgui senban no hito begins the example of an exceedingly upright person. The full Japanese example, including initial R, is upright rather than partly italic.
Nari completes the Japanese predicate. The translation describes a very upright and straightforward person.
Regular adds orderly or proper conduct to the preceding character description. This short line is part of the same example.
Ritō is a sharp sword, surudona katana. The Portuguese supplies Eſpada and Catana as alternative names.
Que corta bem completes the sharp-sword description, specifying effective cutting rather than a separate weapon type.
Ritoku means profits or gains. The example begins Ritocuuo, with a faint but present i; both Japanese spans, including their initial R, are upright.

runs.text: Contender ſobre o intereſſe, ou ganho.

lines.note: Araſô completes the example of contending over profit. The scan supports long s in the Japanese verb and ſobre in Portuguese, not OCR araiô and ſobore.
Ryūka is beneath a willow, yanagi no shita. The headword reads Riǔca rather than OCR Rifica; ſal- begins the Portuguese tree-name.

runs.text: gueiro, ou ao pee do ſalgueiro.

lines.note: Gueiro completes ſalgueiro, followed by the alternative “at the foot of the willow.” The printed pee remains unmodernized.
Ryūkō is the dignity or rank of queen. The u bears a caron in Riǔcǒ; OCR omitted it.
Ryūkotsu is a medicinal substance glossed through the phrase Riôno fone, “dragon’s bone.” The source’s o-vowel in that synonym is retained rather than harmonized with Riǔcot.
Ryūha concerns founding or establishing a school/sect, ha wo tatsuru. The headword is Riǔfa, not the OCR’s Rififa.
Algũa ſeita completes the act of founding a sect. The abbreviation’s tilde remains over u.
Ryūgo is described as an implement shaped like an hourglass. The description, rather than an assumed modern name, governs the interpretation.

runs.text: de area de que vſa o volteador, o qual faz

lines.note: The implement is used by an acrobat, who sets it in motion. De area completes “sand hourglass” from the preceding row.

runs.text: andar à roda, & menea de muitas maneiras

lines.note: The acrobat spins and manipulates the implement in various ways. The printed à is preserved in andar à roda.
A cord is used to operate it; ryūgo nari then describes something of this implement’s shape. The gloss for that compound continues below.
Completes ryūgo nari as the shape or form of the preceding implement. The continuation remains tied to that compound.
Riǔgun is described as a kingdom or polity of dragon-like beings, rendered in Portuguese as lagartos. Preserve the final n in the printed headword.

runs.text: que imaginão os gentios auer dentro do mar.

lines.note: The source attributes belief in this undersea realm to non-Christians. This is the dictionary’s historical description, not an assertion that such a realm exists.
Ryūgan is making a vow, gan wo tatsuru. The Portuguese begins “a vow that one makes,” continued below.
The example Riǔguanuo ſuru means to make a vow. Vt and the Portuguese explanation are italic, while the Japanese phrase is upright.
Ryūgan wo jōju suru means fulfilling the vow. The printed joined jǒjuſuru and historical Comprir are retained.
Ryūjin is defined as the Cami of the dragons. Cami is a Japanese term within the Portuguese gloss and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.
Ryūme is explained by Reôno vonvma and initially glossed as a good horse. The source’s Reôno spelling is preserved rather than normalized.
The horse is also renowned; a second sense concerns the horse ridden by the king. The scan has Caualo em que without the OCR’s extra comma.

runs.text: caualga o Rey. ¶ Item, Hũa certa peça

lines.note: Completes the royal-mount sense and adds a particular game piece. The third sense begins on this physical row.
Do enxadrez completes the reference to a board-game piece. The source’s own terminology is preserved without substituting a modern piece-name.
